options.text: A bias that only affects mutual funds.
A test that includes only companies still listed today, so the companies that failed are missing.
A rule that waits for confirmation before it trades.
A test that trades only the largest companies.

explanations.a: Survivorship bias can affect any test of companies, including stock tests. It is not limited to mutual funds.
explanations.c: Waiting for confirmation is a rule choice. It is not a data bias.
explanations.d: Trading the largest companies is a universe choice. It is not the same as dropping companies that failed.

prompt: Survivorship bias usually makes a test result:

options.text: Look worse than it really was.
Look better than a trader could really have got.
Stay exactly the same as before.
Depend only on how many years the test covers.

explanations.a: Missing the companies that failed removes the losses from the test. The direction is toward a better look.
explanations.c: Removing the companies that failed changes the result. The bias does not leave it unchanged.
explanations.d: The number of years matters for other reasons. Survivorship bias comes from which companies are in the list.

prompt: Hypothetical. You test a rule on today's index members, going back to 2015. What is the main problem?

options.text: The test is too short.
Companies that left the index or were delisted before today are missing, so the universe is biased.
There is no problem, because the index is large.
The test should use a smaller index.

explanations.a: The length of the test is not the main issue here. The list of companies is the issue.
explanations.c: The size of the index does not fix the bias. The companies missing from today's list are still missing.
explanations.d: A smaller index has the same problem. The fix is a point-in-time universe for each past date.

prompt: I used the 50 most liquid stocks today, so my test is representative. Which part is wrong?

options.text: The list comes from today, so stocks that were traded in the past but have since gone are missing.
Liquid stocks cannot be tested at all.
Fifty stocks is too few to test.
Nothing is wrong, because a large list is always representative.

explanations.b: Liquid stocks can be tested. The problem is the list, not the liquidity.
explanations.c: The number of stocks is not the issue. A list of 500 companies from today would have the same problem.
explanations.d: Size does not make a list representative of the past. The list is built from today, so it leaves out the companies that have gone.

prompt: Hypothetical. Four stocks return +50%, +20%, -100% and -40% over the same period. What is the average return of all four, in percent?
Which universe must a test on past dates use?

options.text: Any universe, as long as it is large.
The stocks that existed and could be traded on each past date.
Today's largest stocks.
Only the stocks that have a full history on the source.

explanations.a: Size does not fix the bias. A large list of today's companies still leaves out the companies that have gone.
explanations.c: Today's largest stocks are a survivors-only list. The companies that failed are not in it.
explanations.d: Keeping only the stocks with a full history removes the companies that stopped trading. That is survivorship bias again.
